per_question.hypothesis:
Here are a few practical ways to kick-start fresh ideas for your paintings:

1. Change your subject matter  
  • Pick something you’ve never painted before (e.g. still life if you usually do landscapes, or urban scenes if you do portraits).  
  • Use a random-word generator or flip through a magazine to land on an unexpected theme.

2. Explore new mediums or techniques  
  • If you normally work in acrylic, try gouache, watercolor, oil sticks or even collage.  
  • Experiment with non-traditional tools—palette knives, sponges, toothbrushes, stencils, or found objects.

3. Set playful constraints  
  • Limit yourself to a two- or three-color palette.  
  • Paint at a fixed small size (e.g. thumbnail studies) or super-large scale.  
  • Impose a time limit (make a 10-minute sketch), then refine it later.

4. Get out of the studio  
  • Visit galleries, museums or local art fairs to see what other artists are doing.  
  • Go plein air—paint outside in a park, street corner or botanical garden.  
  • Take photos on a walk, then use them as reference or collage material.

5. Build a mood board or journal  
  • Collect images, color swatches, textures, and phrases that grab your attention.  
  • Keep a sketchbook or visual diary of small doodles, color tests and notes on what moves you.

6. Tap into prompts and challenges  
  • Join online art-a-day challenges (e.g. Inktober, 100-day project).  
  • Follow daily or weekly prompt lists—animals, emotions, unusual color combos—to push your comfort zone.

7. Collaborate and connect  
  • Swap sketches or unfinished work with another artist for them to add to.  
  • Join a local or online critique group to get fresh perspectives.  
  • Take a workshop or class in an unfamiliar style (e.g. printmaking, digital painting).

8. Seek inspiration beyond art  
  • Read poetry or fiction, listen to music or podcasts, and note the emotions or imagery they evoke.  
  • Spend time in nature—study the play of light, texture of bark, pattern of clouds.  
  • Watch films or documentaries for color grading ideas and compositional framing.

9. Play with serendipity  
  • Do “blind” or automatic drawing/painting—close your eyes or work without judgment, then discover shapes and forms in the result.  
  • Tear up old paintings to make spontaneous collages.

10. Reflect on your “why”  
  • Revisit what first drew you to painting—what emotions or ideas you wanted to express.  
  • Jot down feelings you’d like to capture now (e.g. joy, tension, stillness) and let that guide your next pieces.

Hopefully one or two of these jumpstarts a fresh spark. Often the simple act of shaking up routine—new tools, subjects or even a change of scenery—is all it takes to reignite your creativity. Good luck!

per_question.hypothesis:
Here are a few things to keep in mind when you head into the shop:

• Playability and feel  
  – Neck profile and fretboard radius: make sure the neck shape feels good in your hand and allows the fretting hand moves you like.  
  – Body weight and balance: Les Pauls tend to be heavier; Strats lighter. See what you’re comfortable holding for long stretches.  

• Pickups and tonal options  
  – Humbuckers vs. single-coils: humbuckers (Les Paul) will give you a thicker, warmer tone; single-coils (Strat) are brighter and chime-y.  
  – Coil-tap / coil-splitting: if you’re tempted by extra versatility (especially for open D or more “Strat-like” tones), try one with a push-pull pot or mini-toggle to split your humbuckers.  

• Tuning and setup  
  – Try both standard and open D on each guitar, plug in and listen for any fret buzz, dead spots or intonation issues that might show up when you retune.  
  – Pay attention to action and string height—low enough for comfort and fingerstyle work (think “Blackbird”-type picking), but high enough to avoid buzzing.  

• Hardware and build quality  
  – Tuning machines: smooth, stable tuners are a must—open D tuning can be a bit more demanding on your tuners.  
  – Bridge and nut: check for solid construction and proper lubrication at the nut slots so strings don’t bind when you bend or retune.  

• Your ear and your hands  
  – Bring any amps or pedals you’ll use most often, or ask to plug into something similar so you know exactly how it will sit in your rig.  
  – Spend time actually playing through riffs or songs you know well (rhythm, leads, fingerpicking) to get a real feel for whether it inspires you.  

Above all, trust your hands and ears—if it feels and sounds right, you’ve probably found a winner. Have fun at the store!

Here are a few simple tips that might help calm your nerves when getting around Tokyo:

1. Rely on your Suica card  
   • Keep it topped up so you can just tap in and out—no fumbling for tickets.  
   • You can use it not only on trains and buses, but also at many convenience stores and vending machines.  

2. Plan and track your routes in advance  
   • You’ve already got TripIt—add each train segment (line name + exit number) to your itinerary so you know exactly where to go.  
   • Supplement with Google Maps or the “Tokyo Subway Navigation” app; both show real‐time departure times and platform information.  

3. Look for English signage and colored line markers  
   • Station signs are in English + Japanese, and each train line has a distinct color and letter/number code (e.g. “Marunouchi Line M-09”).  
   • Follow the colored line icons on walls and floors to guide you to the correct platform.  

4. Ask station staff if you’re unsure  
   • Every major station has an “Information” window—staff usually speak at least basic English and can point you in the right direction or even write down directions in Japanese.  

5. Build in extra time (and avoid rush hour if you can)  
   • Tokyo’s trains can be very busy between about 7–9 AM and 5–7 PM. If you’re anxious, try traveling slightly before or after those windows.  
   • Arriving 10–15 minutes early gives you a buffer to find your platform calmly.  

6. Use your hotel’s concierge  
   • The Park Hyatt Tokyo’s concierge can print out route maps or even arrange private car transfers if you prefer door-to-door service.  

With your Suica card loaded, TripIt keeping you organized, and these simple strategies, you’ll find Tokyo’s transit system actually quite user-friendly. Enjoy your trip!
